children.title: Search Fairness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure when unresolved regions can remain indefinitely unprocessed.

children.title: Unresolved-Region Starvation
children.top_down_role: Persistent neglect of regions that retain unresolved global-search potential.

knowledge_statements.title: Unresolved-Region Starvation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete failure caused by permanently ignoring an optimizer-containing region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=[0,1]\) and \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\), so \(f^*=0\) at \(x=1\). Split \(X\) into \(B_0=[0,1/2]\) and \(R=[1/2,1]\), retain \(R\) as unresolved with valid lower bound \(L(R)=0\), but thereafter refine and sample only descendants of \(B_0\). Every sampled point then lies in \([0,1/2]\), and hence every incumbent satisfies
\[
U_k\geq\min_{x\in[0,1/2]}(x-1)^2=\tfrac14.
\]
Thus local refinement can continue indefinitely while the incumbent fails to approach the global optimum because the unresolved region containing the optimizer is starved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refining only the left half of an interval can miss a minimizer in a permanently unresolved right-half region.
assumptions_latex: \(R=[1/2,1]\) remains unresolved and is never processed.
All sampled points belong to \([0,1/2]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_k\geq1/4>f^*=0\) for every \(k\).

notation.meaning: starved region containing the global minimizer
best sampled value through iteration k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is algebraically correct and its content kind fits the failure leaf, but it has no cited evidence or explicit standard-field rationale. A source addressing starvation or unfair spatial search is required before candidate-review acceptance.

children.title: Persistent Node Deferral
children.top_down_role: Queue behavior allowing eligible nodes to remain unprocessed without a finite service horizon.

assumptions_latex: For every integer \(k\geq k_0\), \(\mathcal A_k\) is the complete active-node pool and \(U_k\) is the incumbent value.
The region \(R\in\mathcal A_k\) remains active, is never processed or validly pruned, and retains the valid lower bound \(L(R)\).
A fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \(L(R)<U_k-\varepsilon\) for every \(k\geq k_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_k-\min_{B\in\mathcal A_k}L(B)>\varepsilon\) for every \(k\geq k_0\), so complete-pool \(\varepsilon\)-certification cannot occur while these conditions persist.

notation.meaning: complete active-node pool at iteration k
retained valid lower bound for R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification remains blocked while a persistently deferred active node continues to violate the target cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(k\geq k_0\), let \(\mathcal A_k\) be the complete active-node pool and let \(U_k\) be the incumbent value. Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Suppose a region \(R\) remains in \(\mathcal A_k\) for every \(k\geq k_0\), is never processed or validly pruned, retains a valid lower bound \(L(R)\), and satisfies \(L(R)<U_k-\varepsilon\) for every \(k\geq k_0\). Then \(U_k-\min_{B\in\mathcal A_k}L(B)>\varepsilon\) for every \(k\geq k_0\). Thus a complete-pool \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate cannot be issued while this persistent deferral condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node deferred forever blocks certification for as long as its retained lower bound remains more than epsilon below the current incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Node Deferral

children.title: Coverage Loss from Unfair Search
children.top_down_role: Loss of global refinement coverage caused by biased or incomplete node selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Loss from Unfair Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of global convergence when generated samples omit an open optimizer neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=[0,1]\), let \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\), and suppose an unfair search generates only points \(x_k\in[0,1/2]\), although its local subdivisions within that half become arbitrarily fine. The sampled set is not dense in \(X\) and omits the neighborhood \((1/2,1]\) of the unique optimizer. Therefore
\[
\inf_{k\geq1}f(x_k)\geq\tfrac14>0=f^*.
\]
Hence vanishing cell sizes on the regions actually visited do not imply global convergence: the refinement sequence must preserve coverage, or an equivalent fairness property, over every region that can contain a global optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily fine refinement on only part of the domain does not converge globally when an optimizer neighborhood is never covered.
assumptions_latex: Every generated sample satisfies \(x_k\in[0,1/2]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit counterexample is correct and distinguishes local mesh refinement from global coverage. Its counterexample kind fits the leaf, but no citation or explicit standard-field rationale supports its use as candidate memory.

children.title: Bounded-Domain Finite-Accuracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Finite-accuracy closure under effective refinement of bounded search domains.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is compact and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is \(M\)-Lipschitz for some \(M>0\).
At every integer level \(k\geq0\), every partition cell \(B\) is sampled at \(x_B\in B\) and assigned \(L(B)=f(x_B)-M\operatorname{diam}(B)\).
\(\Delta_k\leq q^k\Delta_0\) for some \(q\in(0,1)\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\) for every integer \(k\geq\max\!\left\{0,\left\lceil\log(M\Delta_0/\varepsilon)/\log(1/q)\right\rceil\right\}\).

global lower bound and incumbent at level k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite epsilon termination from Lipschitz bounds and uniform mesh reduction.

source_refs.locator: 3.6 Finite epsilon-Convergence and epsilon-Global Optimality p. 87

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be \(M\)-Lipschitz for some \(M>0\), and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). At every integer level \(k\geq0\), let each cell \(B\) of a finite partition of \(X\) have a sample \(x_B\in B\) and lower bound \(L(B)=f(x_B)-M\operatorname{diam}(B)\). Suppose \(\Delta_k:=\max_B\operatorname{diam}(B)\leq q^k\Delta_0\) for some \(q\in(0,1)\). With \(U_k:=\min_B f(x_B)\) and \(L_k:=\min_B L(B)\), one has \(0\leq U_k-f^*\leq U_k-L_k\leq M\Delta_k\), where \(f^*:=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\). Consequently, \(U_k-L_k\leq\varepsilon\) for every integer \(k\geq\max\!\left\{0,\left\lceil\log(M\Delta_0/\varepsilon)/\log(1/q)\right\rceil\right\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive target accuracy, geometric mesh reduction on a compact domain gives finite epsilon termination when these Lipschitz lower bounds are used.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Domain Finite-Accuracy Regimes

children.title: Active-Node Pool Closure
children.top_down_role: Termination through certified exhaustion or dismissal of unresolved regions.

assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon\geq0\) is fixed and the terminal-region ledger is a finite cover of \(X\).
Each \(L(D)\) is a valid lower bound and satisfies \(L(D)\geq U-\varepsilon\).
\(U=f(\bar x)\) for a feasible point \(\bar x\in X\), and the active-node pool is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq U-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: valid lower bound retained for D

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\). Let \(X\) be covered by finitely many terminal regions \(D\), each carrying a valid lower bound \(L(D)\leq\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\). Let \(U=f(\bar x)\) for some feasible point \(\bar x\in X\). Suppose the active-node pool is empty and every terminal region was discarded only after satisfying \(L(D)\geq U-\varepsilon\). Then \(U-\varepsilon\leq f^*\leq U\), where \(f^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). The empty active pool together with the retained bound-and-coverage ledger is an \(\varepsilon\)-global-optimality certificate for \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any nonnegative epsilon, an empty active pool certifies epsilon optimality when the retained discarded regions cover the domain and each has a valid lower bound at least U minus epsilon.

children.title: Numerical-Tolerance Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interaction among proof accuracy, feasibility tolerances, and bound tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Tolerance Termination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A tolerance budget converting computed bounds into a rigorous epsilon certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widehat U\) and \(\widehat L\) be computed incumbent and lower-bound values. Suppose bound error satisfies \(f^*\geq\widehat L-\delta_L\), and a point with feasibility violation at most \(\tau\) can be restored to an exactly feasible point \(y\) satisfying \(f(y)\leq\widehat U+\delta_U+\omega(\tau)\), where \(\omega(\tau)\geq0\). Then the stopping condition
\[
\widehat U-\widehat L+\delta_U+\delta_L+\omega(\tau)\leq\varepsilon
\]
certifies \(f(y)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\). Thus proof accuracy, numerical bound errors, and feasibility restoration loss must share one error budget rather than being tested independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Termination is rigorous when the computed gap plus bound errors and feasibility-restoration loss does not exceed the requested accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(f^*\geq\widehat L-\delta_L\) with \(\delta_L\geq0\).
A \(\tau\)-feasible incumbent can be restored to feasible \(y\) with \(f(y)\leq\widehat U+\delta_U+\omega(\tau)\).
\(\delta_U\geq0\) and \(\omega(\tau)\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat U-\widehat L+\delta_U+\delta_L+\omega(\tau)\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow f(y)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: certified numerical errors in the computed bounds
objective loss caused by restoring tau-feasibility

children.title: Polyhedral Finite Exactness

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Finite Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite global search over a finite polyhedral representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\bigcup_{i=1}^m P_i\), where every \(P_i\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty compact polyhedron, and suppose \(f(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\) on \(P_i\), with consistent values on overlaps. If spatial search treats the \(P_i\) as its finite terminal regions and solves each regional linear program exactly unless validly pruned, then it terminates after at most \(m\) regional solves and returns
\[
f^*=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}\left\{\min_{x\in P_i}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i)\right\}.
\]
Hence a finite polyhedral representation with exact regional optimization yields finite exactness, rather than merely asymptotic or finite-accuracy convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union of polyhedral regions with affine regional objectives can be optimized exactly after finitely many exact linear-program solves.

notation.meaning: affine objective representation on region i

children.title: Finite Representation Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Representation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle boundary separating finitely resolvable models from unrestricted continuous objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: No deterministic algorithm using finitely many value queries can always compute the exact minimum of every function in \(C([0,1])\). Indeed, run such an algorithm against \(f_0(x)=0\), and let \(S\subset[0,1]\) be its finite query set. The function \(g(x)=-\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) is continuous and agrees with \(f_0\) at every queried point, while \(\min g<0=\min f_0\). Thus identical finite observations cannot certify both optima; finite exactness requires additional finite representation or structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite value observations cannot certify exact minima for all continuous functions; finite exactness requires additional representational or structural restrictions.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and makes finitely many adaptive value queries.
The objective class contains all functions in \(C([0,1])\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No such algorithm is exact on all of \(C([0,1])\).

notation.meaning: The finite set queried on the zero function.
Distance from x to the finite query set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(x^*\in X\) be a global minimizer with \(f^*=f(x^*)\). There can exist nested regions \(R_{k+1}\subseteq R_k\) containing \(x^*\), valid lower bounds \(L_k\le f^*\), and incumbent upper bounds \(U_k\ge f^*\) such that \(L_k<f^*<U_k\) for every finite \(k\), although \(L_k\uparrow f^*\), \(U_k\downarrow f^*\), and \(\operatorname{diam}(R_k)\to0\). Consequently, convergence of bounds and regions establishes only asymptotic exactness and does not imply a finite iteration at which the exact value or an equality certificate is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a metric-space optimization problem, valid lower and upper bounds and nested regions can converge to the optimum while remaining strictly inexact at every finite iteration, so convergence alone does not give finite certification.

children.title: Dimension-Driven Partition Growth
children.top_down_role: Covering growth associated with high-dimensional continuous domains.

assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(a_i<b_i\), and \(X=\prod_{i=1}^d[a_i,b_i]\).
Partition or covering cells are axis-aligned boxes with every side length at most \(h>0\).
The asymptotic statement holds for a fixed nondegenerate box as \(h\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a fixed nondegenerate box, the required number of cells is \(\Theta(h^{-d})\), equivalently \(\Theta((D/h)^d)\), as \(h\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: Maximum side length of the fixed domain box.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covering-number growth for uniform coordinatewise resolution in a fixed box.

source_refs.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\in\mathbb N\), let \(X=\prod_{i=1}^{d}[a_i,b_i]\subset\mathbb R^d\) with \(a_i<b_i\), and set \(D=\max_i(b_i-a_i)\). An axis-aligned uniform partition whose cells have every side length at most \(h>0\) can be formed with \(\prod_{i=1}^{d}\lceil(b_i-a_i)/h\rceil\le\lceil D/h\rceil^d\) cells. Conversely, any covering of \(X\) by axis-aligned boxes having every side length at most \(h\) uses at least \(\operatorname{vol}(X)/h^d\) cells. Therefore, for fixed \(X\), the cell count required for coordinatewise resolution \(h\) is \(\Theta(h^{-d})\), equivalently \(\Theta((D/h)^d)\), as \(h\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed nondegenerate d-dimensional box, coordinatewise resolution h requires on the order of h to the negative d cells; an explicit grid gives the upper bound and volume gives the matching order lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Driven Partition Growth

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\mathcal R\) be a family of nonempty regions having finite diameter and finite regional infima \(f_R^*=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\). For a finite valid lower bound \(L(R)\le f_R^*\), define the additive relaxation gap by \(g(R)=f_R^*-L(R)\ge0\). A relaxation has strength modulus \(\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) on \(\mathcal R\) if \(g(R)\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}R)\) for every \(R\in\mathcal R\) and \(\omega(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Smaller gaps, or a pointwise smaller modulus, represent stronger regional lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a metric-space optimization problem with finite regional infima, regional relaxation strength is measured by the nonnegative difference between the true regional infimum and a valid finite lower bound; a strength modulus controls that gap by region diameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Size Sensitivity to Bound Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic pruning effect under pointwise stronger lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two minimization searches using the same branching rule, node-selection order, feasible candidates, and pruning test \(L(R)\ge U\), where \(U\) is the common incumbent. If their regional bounds satisfy \(L_2(R)\ge L_1(R)\) for every region that either search can generate, then every region pruned by \(L_1\) is also pruned by \(L_2\). Hence the tree generated with \(L_2\) is a subtree of that generated with \(L_1\), and \(N(T_2)\le N(T_1)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Per-Node Tightening Effort
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational work spent strengthening bounds at one search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a processed node \(v\), let \(e_{m tight}(v)\ge0\) denote the computational resources used to strengthen its regional relaxation, including added cuts, propagation rounds, relaxation refinements, or tighter solves. For a processed-node set \(V_{m proc}\), total tightening effort is \(E_{m tight}=\sum_{v\in V_{m proc}}e_{m tight}(v)\). If \(e_{m tight}(v)\le\bar e_{m tight}\) uniformly, then \(E_{m tight}\le |V_{m proc}|\bar e_{m tight}\). The resource unit must be fixed, such as arithmetic operations or oracle calls.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total work is the sum of enumeration, tightening, and feasible-search costs over generated nodes. children.title: Worst-Case Exponential Search

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Exponential Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive box subdivision when regional bounds provide no pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the initial region be \(X=[0,1]^n\), and let \(0<\delta<1\). Consider a spatial subdivision method whose terminal boxes have every side length at most \(\delta\). If every nonterminal box remains potentially improving, so no box can be pruned before satisfying this resolution, then the terminal boxes cover \(X\) and their number \(L\) satisfies \[L\geq \left\lceil \delta^{-n}\right\rceil.\] Thus attaining fixed coordinate resolution has worst-case tree size exponential in the dimension \(n\); accounting for internal nodes cannot reduce this lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without effective pruning, resolving every coordinate to width δ requires at least δ^{-n} terminal boxes, giving exponential worst-case growth in dimension.
assumptions_latex: No nonterminal region is pruned by bounds, infeasibility, or dominance.
Every terminal box has all side lengths at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\geq\lceil\delta^{-n}\rceil\), hence the required tree size is exponential in \(n\) for fixed \(\delta\).

children.title: Original-Space Spatial Search
children.top_down_role: Branching and regional bounding expressed primarily in original variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Original-Space Spatial Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spatial branch-and-bound conducted solely in the original decision-variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a bounded box, let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:X\to\mathbb R\), and consider \(p^*=\min\{f(x):g_i(x)\leq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in X\}\). Fix \(\varepsilon\geq0\) and initialize the active list with \(X\). At each active box \(B\subseteq X\), construct a valid relaxation expressed only in the original variables \(x\), producing a lower bound \(L(B)\), and use feasible points to update the incumbent value \(U\). Prune \(B\) when infeasibility is certified or \(L(B)\geq U-\varepsilon\); otherwise split an original-variable interval into children whose union covers \(B\), and insert the children. If the active list is nonempty, let \(L_{\mathrm{act}}=\min\{L(B):B\text{ is active}\}\). Terminate when either the active list is empty or \(U-L_{\mathrm{act}}\leq\varepsilon\), provided a finite incumbent exists, and return the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method bounds and partitions boxes directly in the original variables. With valid regional bounds, covering splits, and a finite incumbent, exhausting the active list or closing the active-node gap certifies an absolute global-optimality gap of at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a bounded box and the feasible problem has finite attained optimum \(p^*\).
Every regional relaxation supplies a valid lower bound.
Every split covers its parent without omitting feasible points.
A finite incumbent \(U\) exists when the termination test is applied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On the stated termination conditions, \(U-p^*\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: valid lower bound over box B
smallest lower bound among active boxes

children.title: Lifted Expression-Space Spatial Search
children.top_down_role: Search using auxiliary variables and explicit expression-graph relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Expression-Space Spatial Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spatial search over an explicit lifted representation of a factorable expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent each composite factorable expression by auxiliary variables \(z_v\) and graph relations \(z_v=\phi_v(z_{pa(v)})\), with original variables at the leaves. Initialize bounds for \((x,z)\), construct valid convex relaxations of every graph relation, and solve the lifted relaxation for a lower bound. If the node is not pruned, branch on an original or auxiliary interval, propagate the new bounds through the graph, and rebuild affected relaxations. Feasible original points update the incumbent. Terminate when all nodes are pruned or the lifted-tree lower bound is within \(\varepsilon\) of the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables expose the expression graph so its relations can be relaxed, propagated, and spatially partitioned within one global-search tree.
assumptions_latex: The factorable formulation has a finite acyclic expression graph.
Each graph-relation relaxation is valid over its current bounds.
Lifted feasibility projects to feasibility of the original formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maintained node bound is valid for the original problem, and gap termination yields an \(\varepsilon\)-global incumbent.

notation.meaning: auxiliary value of expression-graph node v
parents supplying the arguments of graph node v

children.title: Mixed Discrete–Spatial Branching
children.top_down_role: Coordination of integer disjunctions and continuous-domain subdivisions.

children.title: Integrality-Priority Branching
children.top_down_role: Policies prioritizing unresolved integer structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Priority Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic branching policy that resolves fractional integer variables before spatial candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a mixed-integer spatial-search node, solve the node relaxation and obtain \((\bar x,\bar z)\). If some integer-restricted component satisfies \(\bar x_j\notin\mathbb Z\), select an eligible such component and create children imposing \(x_j\leq\lfloor\bar x_j\rfloor\) and \(x_j\geq\lceil\bar x_j\rceil\). Spatial branching is considered only when every integer-restricted component of the relaxation solution is integral or no valid integer candidate remains. Each child inherits all other regional restrictions and is subsequently bounded and propagated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever the relaxation is fractional, branch on an integer variable first; use spatial branching only after integrality candidates are exhausted.
assumptions_latex: The node relaxation has an optimal solution \((\bar x,\bar z)\).
Integer-variable bounds are integral.
Both integer disjunction children are intersected with the parent region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every fractional integer relaxation solution is excluded by the selected disjunction while the parent integer-feasible set remains covered.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integer-first disjunction is mathematically standard and fits the algorithm container, but no inspectable source supports this specific MINLP priority policy.

children.title: Cross-Type Branching Candidate Selection
children.top_down_role: Policies comparing discrete and continuous branching candidates together.

children.title: Integer Branching Candidates
children.top_down_role: Discrete branching options considered within unified candidate pools.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Branching Candidates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eligible discrete disjunctions identified from a mixed-integer node relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be the indices of integer-restricted variables and let \(\bar x\) solve the current node relaxation. The integer branching-candidate set is \[\mathcal C_I(\bar x)=\{j\in I:\ell_j<\bar x_j<u_j,\ \bar x_j\notin\mathbb Z\}.\] Each \(j\in\mathcal C_I(\bar x)\) defines the exhaustive disjunction \(x_j\leq\lfloor\bar x_j\rfloor\) or \(x_j\geq\lceil\bar x_j\rceil\), after intersecting both sides with the current integral bounds \([\ell_j,u_j]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer branching candidate is an integer-restricted variable whose node-relaxation value is fractional and lies strictly inside its current bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) indexes integer-restricted variables.
\(\ell_j,u_j\in\mathbb Z\) are current valid bounds for every \(j\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(j\in\mathcal C_I(\bar x)\), the two branches cover all integer-feasible parent points and exclude \(\bar x_j\).

notation.meaning: current bounds of integer variable j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fractional integer-candidate definition and covering disjunction are precise and appropriate, but the record has no cited source with a locator.

children.title: Spatial Branching Candidates
children.top_down_role: Continuous-domain partition candidates considered within unified candidate pools.

knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Branching Candidates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eligible bounded variables whose partition can tighten a nonconvex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a node with relaxation solution \((\bar x,\bar z)\), let \(W_k=[\ell_k,u_k]\) be the current interval of a bounded original or lifted variable. Given a positive resolution \(\eta_k\) and a nonconvex-relation set \(R_k\) involving that variable, define \[\mathcal C_S=\{k:u_k-\ell_k>\eta_k,\ R_k\neq\varnothing,\ \max_{r\in R_k}v_r(\bar x,\bar z)>0\}.\] Here \(v_r\) is a nonnegative relaxation-discrepancy measure. Any \(k\in\mathcal C_S\) may be split at an interior point into intervals whose union is \(W_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spatial candidate has nontrivial width, participates in a nonconvex relation, and exhibits positive relaxation discrepancy at the current solution.
assumptions_latex: Every candidate variable has finite current bounds.
Each discrepancy \(v_r\) is nonnegative and vanishes when relation \(r\) is exact.
Every split point lies strictly inside the candidate interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branching on \(k\in\mathcal C_S\) covers the parent region and permits tighter relation relaxations on its children.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is one policy-dependent candidate definition rather than a universal definition. Positive pointwise discrepancy and interval splitting permit rebuilding relaxations but do not alone guarantee a strictly tighter child relaxation; a specific source and corresponding hypotheses are required.

children.title: Cross-Type Candidate Scoring
children.top_down_role: Comparable ranking criteria for discrete versus spatial branching opportunities.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Type Candidate Scoring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparable scoring of integer and spatial branching candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every candidate \(c\in\mathcal C_I\cup\mathcal C_S\), estimate nonnegative child-bound improvements \(\widehat\Delta_c^-\) and \(\widehat\Delta_c^+\) using strong branching, pseudocosts, or a validated surrogate. Choose fixed \(\mu\in[0,1]\) and a positive scale \(d_c\), and compute \[S(c)=\frac{(1-\mu)\min\{\widehat\Delta_c^-,\widehat\Delta_c^+\}+\mu\max\{\widehat\Delta_c^-,\widehat\Delta_c^+\}}{d_c}.\] Select any maximizer of \(S\), with a deterministic tie rule. The same scaling convention must be applied to integer and spatial candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Predict both child-bound gains, normalize them comparably across candidate types, and branch on the candidate with the largest combined score.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C_I\cup\mathcal C_S\neq\varnothing\).
All predicted gains are finite and nonnegative.
Every normalization scale satisfies \(d_c>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected candidate belongs to \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c\in\mathcal C_I\cup\mathcal C_S}S(c)\).

notation.meaning: predicted lower-bound improvements of the two children

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local role fit, but the proposed normalized min-max formula is only one scoring family, and neither the cross-type normalization nor the meaning of a validated surrogate is sourced.

children.title: Candidate-Priority Regimes
children.top_down_role: Policies shifting preference among candidate types as tree conditions change.

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate-Priority Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal regimes controlling competition between integer and spatial candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_I\) and \(S_S\) be the largest finite scores among integer and spatial candidates, with the maximum of an empty set equal to \(-\infty\). An integer-priority regime selects an integer candidate whenever \(\mathcal C_I\neq\varnothing\); a spatial-priority regime analogously selects spatial candidates first. A balanced regime fixes positive weights \(w_I,w_S\) and selects the type maximizing \(w_I S_I\) versus \(w_S S_S\). Within the selected type, a maximum-score candidate is chosen using a fixed tie rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Priority may be lexicographically integer-first, spatial-first, or balanced by weighted comparison of the best score from each candidate class.
assumptions_latex: At least one of \(\mathcal C_I\) and \(\mathcal C_S\) is nonempty.
Candidate scores are finite within each nonempty class.
Balanced-regime weights satisfy \(w_I,w_S>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each regime defines a deterministic candidate type and, with fixed tie breaking, a deterministic branch candidate.

notation.meaning: best integer and spatial candidate scores

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalization of common priority policies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three regimes are a plausible formalization but are unsupported by a citation. The balanced regime also lacks a tie rule when the two weighted type scores are equal, so its determinism conclusion is not established as written.

children.title: Early Spatial Refinement
children.top_down_role: Policies refining dominant nonlinearities before extensive integer enumeration.

knowledge_statements.title: Early Spatial Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spatial-first policy used while nonlinear relaxation error remains dominant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a discrepancy threshold \(\tau>0\) and define the node discrepancy \(V=\max_r v_r(\bar x,\bar z)\). After solving and propagating a node relaxation, if \(V>\tau\) and \(\mathcal C_S\neq\varnothing\), select a maximum-score spatial candidate even when integer candidates exist. Otherwise apply the designated integer or cross-type branching rule. Each spatial split must cover the parent interval, and all children are rebound before further selection. The policy therefore refines dominant nonlinearities until their measured discrepancy is at most \(\tau\) or no spatial candidate remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: While nonlinear relaxation discrepancy exceeds a threshold, choose spatial refinement before integer enumeration; afterward revert to the ordinary branching policy.
assumptions_latex: The discrepancy measures \(v_r\) are finite and nonnegative.
Every spatial split preserves coverage of the parent feasible set.
A fallback branching rule is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(V>\tau\) and \(\mathcal C_S\neq\varnothing\), the next selected branch is spatial.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the early-refinement container, but the threshold policy is formulation-specific and unsourced. The range of the maximum defining the node discrepancy is also not introduced.

children.title: Global MINLP Tree Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Integrated and decomposed organizations of discrete and spatial global search.

children.title: Single-Tree Global MINLP Search
children.top_down_role: Integrated discrete branching, spatial branching, relaxation, and propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Tree Global MINLP Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One tree integrates discrete and spatial disjunctions for bounded factorable MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize one active tree with the bounded MINLP root region. At each node, propagate bounds and solve a valid relaxation to obtain lower bound \(L_N\); use feasible solutions to update incumbent \(U\). Prune nodes certified infeasible or satisfying \(L_N\geq U-\varepsilon\). Otherwise select either an integer disjunction or a spatial interval split, create covering children, and return them to the same active tree. Continue until no node remains with lower bound below \(U-\varepsilon\). The returned incumbent then has objective value within \(\varepsilon\) of the global optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single branch-and-bound tree interleaves integer and spatial branching while sharing propagation, relaxations, bounds, and the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: The MINLP has bounded variable domains and a finite global optimum.
Every node relaxation gives a valid lower bound.
Branching children cover every feasible point of their parent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, the incumbent satisfies \(U-p^*\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: valid lower bound at node N

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical integrated spatial branch-and-bound scheme

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriate single-tree algorithmic scheme, and its certification claim is conditionally standard, but no authoritative MINLP source is cited. Bounded domains and covering branches alone do not establish finite termination.

children.title: Multitree Global MINLP Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Master-level discrete search coordinated with subsidiary global nonlinear searches.

knowledge_statements.title: Multitree Global MINLP Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A discrete master tree coordinates separate globally solved nonlinear subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a master tree over integer assignments or integer-domain restrictions. For each master node \(M\), invoke a subsidiary spatial global-search tree on the associated continuous nonconvex subproblem and require it to return either infeasibility, a feasible solution, or a certified lower bound \(L_M\). Update the common incumbent \(U\), prune \(M\) when infeasible or when \(L_M\geq U-\varepsilon\), and otherwise refine the master restriction or resume subsidiary searches. Terminate only when every open master node has a certified bound at least \(U-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master discrete tree delegates nonlinear subproblems to separate spatial-search trees and uses their certified bounds for global pruning.
assumptions_latex: Master nodes collectively cover all admissible integer assignments.
Each subsidiary search returns a valid bound or certified infeasibility.
All trees share a valid incumbent value \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Master termination certifies \(U-p^*\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: certified bound returned for master node M

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The description plausibly represents a multitree framework, but several distinct master/subproblem organizations are blended without a source. The accuracy and coordination requirements for subsidiary bounds need authoritative support.

children.title: Hybrid Global MINLP Frameworks
children.top_down_role: Spatial search combined with cutting planes, decomposition, or specialized relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Global MINLP Frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spatial search strengthened by globally valid cuts, decomposition, or specialized relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each active MINLP region \(N\), construct a lower-bounding relaxation from valid convex envelopes together with any globally or regionally valid cutting planes, decomposition bounds, and specialized relaxations. Solve it for \(L_N\), propagate implications, and update incumbent \(U\) from feasible points. Prune if infeasibility is certified or \(L_N\geq U-\varepsilon\); otherwise add valid strengthening information or apply an integer or spatial branch whose children cover \(N\). Continue until every active region is pruned by the common incumbent-gap test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The framework combines spatial branching with valid cuts, decomposition bounds, or specialized relaxations while retaining global lower-bound and coverage guarantees.
assumptions_latex: Every added cut or decomposition bound is valid on the region where it is used.
Every node relaxation lower-bounds the original objective over that region.
Every branch covers the parent feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the algorithm terminates with incumbent \(U\), then \(U-p^*\leq\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the hybrid-framework container at a high level, but it combines cutting-plane, decomposition, and specialized-relaxation variants without an authoritative citation. Its optimality statement is valid only conditionally on the stated termination and bound-validity properties.

children.title: Verified Interval Spatial Search
children.top_down_role: Verified regional search using interval enclosures, contractors, and box subdivision.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Section 2.3: Algorithms Based on Interval Methods

children.title: Interval Objective Bounds
children.top_down_role: Regional objective enclosures used for global pruning.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Objective Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion bounds for pruning boxes in verified minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a box, let \(D\supseteq X\), and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). An interval extension \(F\) is inclusion isotonic and satisfies \(f(x)\in F(X)=[\underline F(X),\overline F(X)]\) for every \(x\in X\). Consequently, \(\underline F(X)\leq\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\leq\sup_{x\in X}f(x)\leq\overline F(X)\). In a minimization search with incumbent value \(U\), the box \(X\) may be discarded whenever \(\underline F(X)\geq U\), without removing any point having objective value below \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid interval enclosure bounds every objective value in a box; the box is safely pruned when its lower bound cannot improve the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is contained in the domain of \(f\).
\(F(X)\) is computed with outward rounding or another inclusion-preserving procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\underline F(X)\geq U\Rightarrow f(x)\geq U\) for all \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of the objective range on the box
objective value of a feasible incumbent

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically precise and fits the interval-bound leaf, but it has no source reference. An authoritative interval-analysis or verified-global-optimization source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Interval Constraint Contractors
children.top_down_role: Verified feasibility contraction and exclusion within regional boxes.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Constraint Contractors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verified contraction for constraint systems over boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a constraint set \(S=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\leq0,\ i\in I;\ h_j(x)=0,\ j\in J\}\), a contractor is a map \(C\) from boxes in \(D\) to boxes such that \(C(X)\subseteq X\) and \(X\cap S\subseteq C(X)\). Thus \(C(X)=\varnothing\) certifies \(X\cap S=\varnothing\), while a nonempty result removes only points that cannot satisfy the constraints. A contractor is idempotent when \(C(C(X))=C(X)\), although idempotence is not required for verified exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contractor shrinks a box while retaining every feasible point; an empty contracted box is a verified infeasibility result.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and every input box lies in \(D\).
All numerical tests used by \(C\) are inclusion preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\cap S\subseteq C(X)\subseteq X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The contractor definition and empty-box exclusion implication are standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Verified Interval Certificates
children.top_down_role: Global certificates supported by safe enclosures and validated feasibility information.

knowledge_statements.title: Verified Interval Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite certificates for global lower bounds and optimality gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f\) over a feasible set \(S\subseteq X_0\). A verified interval certificate consists of a feasible point \(\hat x\in S\), its rigorously rounded upper bound \(U\geq f(\hat x)\), and finitely many boxes \(X_k\) covering \(S\), each either proved infeasible by a verified contractor or assigned a valid objective lower bound \(L_k\leq\inf_{x\in X_k\cap S}f(x)\). If every nonexcluded box satisfies \(L_k\geq U-\varepsilon\), then \(f(\hat x)-\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\leq\varepsilon\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), \(\hat x\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent plus a verified finite cover proves global epsilon-optimality when every surviving box has lower bound at least incumbent minus epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\bigcup_k X_k\).
All feasibility exclusions, objective bounds, and incumbent evaluations are inclusion preserving.
\(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq f(\hat x)-\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\leq\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-cover certificate is internally consistent and the certificate content kind is appropriate, but its global optimality claim requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Regularity-Covering Global Search
children.top_down_role: Spatial search using regularity-based regional bounds and adaptive coverings.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Section 2.7: Partition Strategies in General Lipschitz Optimization

children.title: Univariate Lipschitz Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Interval-based adaptive search in one dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Lipschitz Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piyavskii-type deterministic partitioning with a known Lipschitz constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\), a Lipschitz constant \(L>0\), and a tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), initialize the sampled endpoints and their induced interval partition. For each adjacent sampled pair \(x_i<x_{i+1}\), compute \(R_i=\min_{x\in[x_i,x_{i+1}]}\max\{f(x_i)-L(x-x_i),f(x_{i+1})-L(x_{i+1}-x)\}\). Select an interval attaining the smallest \(R_i\), sample at the intersection of its two affine minorants, and update the partition and incumbent \(U\). Stop when \(U-\min_iR_i\leq\varepsilon\); then return the best sampled point and the certified lower bound \(\min_iR_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly split the interval whose Lipschitz minorant has the lowest value, and stop when the certified global lower bound is within tolerance of the best sampled value.
assumptions_latex: \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L|x-y|\) for all \(x,y\in[a,b]\).
The function evaluations used in the displayed minorants and incumbent are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq U-\inf_{x\in[a,b]}f(x)\leq\varepsilon\) at termination.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz lower bound on partition interval i

children.title: Multivariate Lipschitz Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Rectangular, simplicial, and general-set coverings in multiple dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multivariate Lipschitz Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound search over a finite cover in a normed Euclidean domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact and covered by finitely many regions \(Q\). For each region choose a representative \(c_Q\in Q\), evaluate \(f(c_Q)\), and set \(B(Q)=f(c_Q)-Lr(Q)\), where \(r(Q)=\sup_{x\in Q}\|x-c_Q\|\). Maintain \(U\), the best feasible sampled value. Repeatedly select a region with minimal \(B(Q)\), subdivide it into finitely many covering children, evaluate their representatives, and update bounds. Stop when \(U-\min_QB(Q)\leq\varepsilon\); output the incumbent and lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cover the domain by regions, bound each from its center and radius, and repeatedly subdivide the region with the most promising lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in D\).
Every subdivision's children cover their parent.
\(D\) is compact and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(Q)\leq\inf_{x\in Q}f(x)\) for every active region \(Q\).

notation.meaning: covering radius of region Q about its representative
Lipschitz lower bound for region Q

children.title: Unknown or Estimated Regularity Parameters
children.top_down_role: Search regimes where bound validity or efficiency depends on estimated regularity information.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown or Estimated Regularity Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for Lipschitz lower bounds using an estimated constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) have true Lipschitz modulus \(L_*\) with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\), and let a regional bound be \(B_{\widehat L}(Q)=f(c_Q)-\widehat Lr(Q)\). If \(\widehat L\geq L_*\), then \(B_{\widehat L}(Q)\leq\inf_{x\in Q}f(x)\) for every region \(Q\). If \(\widehat L<L_*\), this guarantee fails: for \(D=[0,1]\), \(Q=D\), \(c_Q=0\), and \(f(x)=-L_*x\), one obtains \(B_{\widehat L}(Q)=-\widehat L> -L_*=\inf_Q f\). Hence pruning based solely on an underestimated modulus is not globally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimated Lipschitz bounds are safe only when the estimate dominates the true modulus; underestimation can make lower bounds exceed the actual minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is contained in a normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat L<L_*\) can invalidate both regional lower bounds and pruning decisions.

notation.meaning: radius of region Q about its representative

children.title: Cover Geometry Selection
children.top_down_role: Regional cover shapes, overlap policies, plus geometric resolution choices used in global search.

knowledge_statements.title: Cover Geometry Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry-dependent tightness of Lipschitz regional bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an \(L\)-Lipschitz function on a nonempty compact region \(Q\), any representative \(c\in Q\) yields the valid lower bound \(f(c)-Lr_Q(c)\), where \(r_Q(c)=\sup_{x\in Q}\|x-c\|\). Selecting a restricted Chebyshev center \(c_Q\in\arg\min_{c\in Q}r_Q(c)\) minimizes the worst-case radius correction \(Lr_Q(c)\) among representatives in \(Q\). It does not in general maximize the complete bound \(f(c)-Lr_Q(c)\), since the sampled value \(f(c)\) also depends on \(c\). Cover shapes may therefore be compared through their covering radii in the norm defining regularity, together with their ability to preserve complete coverage under subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose cover shapes and representatives with small covering radius in the Lipschitz norm, while recognizing that the sampled function value also affects the resulting lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in Q\).
\(Q\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(c_Q\in\arg\min_{c\in Q}r_Q(c)\), then \(Lr_Q(c_Q)\leq Lr_Q(c)\) for every \(c\in Q\).

notation.meaning: maximum distance from representative c to region Q

children.title: Adaptive Cover Refinement
children.top_down_role: Cover evolution driven by regional promise, regularity information, plus unresolved spatial gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Cover Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-bound refinement of a regularity-based finite cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a finite cover \(\mathcal Q_0\) of a compact domain \(D\), valid regional lower bounds \(B(Q)\), sampled representatives \(c_Q\in Q\), and an incumbent \(U\). At iteration \(k\), discard every \(Q\in\mathcal Q_k\) satisfying \(B(Q)\geq U-\varepsilon\). Select a surviving region with minimal bound, replace it by finitely many children whose union covers it, evaluate their required representatives, compute valid child bounds, and update \(U\). Return the incumbent when no region survives. If, whenever the process does not terminate, the maximum diameter of the surviving active regions tends to zero and \(0\leq f(c_Q)-B(Q)\leq\omega(\operatorname{diam}Q)\) for a function \(\omega(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\), then the lower-bound gap closes and the procedure terminates with an \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal incumbent for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refine the region with the best lower bound and prune regions unable to improve the incumbent. Global tolerance certification follows when the active cover becomes uniformly fine and its regional bounds become uniformly exact.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is compact, and every active family covers all unpruned points.
Each \(B(Q)\) is a valid lower bound on \(Q\), and every representative \(c_Q\) lies in \(Q\).
If the process does not terminate, the maximum diameter of the surviving active regions tends to zero.
There is a function \(\omega\) with \(\omega(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\) such that \(0\leq f(c_Q)-B(Q)\leq\omega(\operatorname{diam}Q)\) for every active region.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(0\leq U-\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: active regional cover at iteration k
valid lower bound for region Q

children.top_down_role: Spatial branch-and-bound specializations for recurring nonconvex structures.

children.title: Product-Structured Program Family
children.top_down_role: Spatial refinement driven by product relaxations and variable domains.

children.title: Bilinear Programs
children.top_down_role: Spatial search for models whose nonconvex structure is dominated by pairwise products.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional programs whose nonconvexity includes products of two variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilinear program is an optimization problem over variables \(x\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^q\) in which every objective and constraint function is affine plus bilinear, namely \(\phi(x,y)=a+b^\top x+c^\top y+x^\top Qy\), with coefficients depending on the function. Linear constraints and variable bounds are included by taking \(Q=0\). In spatial global optimization, auxiliary variables \(w_{ij}=x_i y_j\) expose each nonconvex product so that convex relaxations can be formed over bounded rectangles and tightened by branching on factor domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear program has objectives and constraints containing products between two variable blocks, commonly exposed through auxiliary product variables for relaxation and branching.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are finite-dimensional real vectors.
Domains used for bounded product relaxations provide finite lower and upper bounds on the factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each nonlinear term has the form \(x_i y_j\) after expanding \(x^\top Qy\).

notation.meaning: auxiliary variable representing the product of two factors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional affine-plus-bilinear definition fits the Bilinear Programs leaf, but the record supplies no source for either the terminology or the stated spatial-relaxation treatment.

children.title: Multilinear Programs
children.top_down_role: Spatial search for models containing products across three or more variable factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Programs with products affine in each variable block separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let variables be partitioned into blocks \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)}\). A function \(p\) is multilinear if, for every block index \(k\), the map \(x^{(k)}\mapsto p(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})\) is affine when all other blocks are fixed. A multilinear program has an objective and constraint functions of this form, possibly together with linear functions. In scalar coordinates, every monomial is square-free, so it has the form \(c_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i\). Bilinear programs are the special case in which each nonlinear monomial has degree at most two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilinear program is affine in each variable block when all other blocks are fixed; its scalar monomials contain no repeated variable.
assumptions_latex: All variable blocks are finite-dimensional real vectors.
The block partition is fixed throughout the formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is affine separately in every block \(x^{(k)}\).

notation.meaning: coefficient of a square-free scalar monomial

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is plausible, but multilinearity conventions differ between scalar variables and vector blocks. A source is needed to confirm the intended block convention and the characterization of bilinear programs as the degree-two special case.

children.title: Product-Relaxation Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Regional relaxation choices linking direct multilinear treatment with recursive product representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Relaxation Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested convex relaxations obtained by recursively exposing and partitioning product terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a bounded product-structured minimization problem with feasible set \(S\) and optimum \(v^*\). At relaxation level \(r\), introduce auxiliary variables for selected products, impose valid convex envelopes on the current factor boxes, and let \(R_r\) be the resulting convex feasible region with optimum \(v_r\). If added constraints or refined boxes satisfy \(S\subseteq R_{r+1}\subseteq R_r\), then \(v_r\leq v_{r+1}\leq v^*\). When every product envelope becomes exact along refinement, every accumulation value of the nondecreasing lower-bound sequence equals \(v^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested convex product relaxations yield nondecreasing lower bounds, converging to the global optimum when all product envelopes become exact under refinement.
assumptions_latex: The original factor domains are bounded.
Every imposed product envelope is valid on its associated factor box.
Refinement makes all envelope gaps vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_r\leq v_{r+1}\leq v^*\) and \(\lim_{r\to\infty}v_r=v^*\).

notation.meaning: convex relaxation feasible region at level r
relaxation lower bound at level r
global optimum of the original minimization problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonicity and convergence assertions are theorem-like rather than a generic property. Exactness of individual envelopes along unspecified refinement is also insufficient by itself to establish convergence of relaxation optima; the hierarchy variant, compactness or attainment conditions, and convergence mechanism require authoritative sourcing.

children.title: Indefinite Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Spatial search using quadratic-specific bounds and branching criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded quadratic optimization with an indefinite objective or constraint Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For indices \(i=0,1,\ldots,m\), let \(q_i(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Q_ix+c_i^\top x+d_i\), where \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and each \(Q_i\) is symmetric. An indefinite quadratic program minimizes \(q_0(x)\) subject to \(q_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), together with any stated linear constraints, and has at least one formulation-relevant matrix \(Q_i\) with both a negative and a positive eigenvalue. If \(Q_0\) is indefinite, then the objective is neither convex nor concave on any convex domain with nonempty interior. Spatial global methods may construct convex underestimators on bounded regions, compute regional lower bounds, and branch until a prescribed global optimality gap is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite quadratic program has an objective or quadratic constraint with both positive and negative curvature; spatial methods can bound such terms by convex underestimators over bounded regions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and all variables and coefficients are finite-dimensional and real.
Every quadratic coefficient matrix is represented by its symmetric part.
Regions used for finite spatial envelopes are bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_i\) is indefinite exactly when \(\lambda_{\min}(Q_i)<0<\lambda_{\max}(Q_i)\).

notation.meaning: symmetric Hessian matrix of quadratic function i

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

children.title: Separated-Nonconvexity Program Family
children.top_down_role: Partition and cut-and-split methods organized around separated nonconvexity.

children.title: Difference-of-Convex Programs
children.top_down_role: Spatial treatment of models expressed through separated convex components.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(g_i,h_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex for \(i=0,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The program is a difference-of-convex program because every objective and constraint function is expressed as a difference of two convex functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constrained DC formulation used in deterministic global optimization.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Difference of Convex (D.C.) Functions p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A difference-of-convex program has the form \[\inf_{x\in C}\; g_0(x)-h_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)-h_i(x)\leq 0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where each \(g_i\) and \(h_i\) is convex on \(C\). The displayed decomposition is part of the formulation and need not be unique. Affine equalities and convex constraints are included by taking an appropriate convex component to be zero or affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC program minimizes a difference of convex functions subject to constraints that are also expressed as convex-function differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Difference-of-Convex Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Difference of Convex (D.C.) Functions p. 58

children.title: Reverse-Convex Programs
children.top_down_role: Spatial treatment of feasible regions containing reversed convex inequalities.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty convex set.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(g_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each inequality \(g_i(x)\geq 0\) is reverse-convex: its excluded strict sublevel set is convex, while its feasible side may be nonconvex.
review_flags: A source specifically supporting the selected reverse-convex convention and hypotheses is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention that a convex function is constrained to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reverse-convex program has the form \[\inf_{x\in C} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\geq 0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m.\] For every \(i\), the forbidden set \(\{x\in C:g_i(x)<0\}\) is convex, although the feasible set \(C\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(x)\geq0\}\) generally is not. Variants may additionally include ordinary convex constraints without changing which inequalities carry the reverse-convex structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex program imposes nonnegative lower bounds on convex functions, producing feasible regions that are generally nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Convex Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated reverse-convex convention is mathematically plausible and the definition kind fits the leaf, but no citation supports the selected sign convention, multiple-constraint formulation, or hypotheses.

children.title: Component-Based Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Refinement organized around selected nonconvex components or component domains.

assumptions_latex: A node domain \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact.
The relaxation gap decomposes as nonnegative component gaps \(\Delta_j(B)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned children cover \(B\), and every child relaxation remains a valid lower-bounding relaxation of the corresponding regional problem.

notation.meaning: Relaxation gap attributed to component j.

review_flags: A source is needed for this component-gap partitioning specification and its validity conditions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic component-selection rule for spatial relaxations with decomposable nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(B\), compute or estimate \(\Delta_j(B)\) for every nonconvex component and choose \(j^*\in\arg\max_j\Delta_j(B)\). Select a variable or component parameter affecting \(j^*\), and construct finitely many child domains \(B_1,\ldots,B_q\) satisfying \(B=\bigcup_{r=1}^q B_r\) with disjoint interiors. Recompute valid regional estimators for the selected component on each child and retain every unchanged valid estimator. Stop when the node is fathomed or all component gaps meet prescribed tolerances; otherwise repeat on a selected child.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the domain where a nonconvex component contributes the largest relaxation gap, then rebuild its regional estimator on covering children.
knowledge_statements.title: Component-Based Partitioning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits component-based partitioning, but the component-gap selection rule and conditions ensuring valid inherited and recomputed estimators have no cited support.

children.title: Split-Cut Search Regimes
children.top_down_role: Global-search regimes combining regional disjunctions with relaxation-strengthening cuts.

assumptions_latex: Each active node \(B\) has a valid lower-bounding relaxation.
Every split produces finitely many children whose union is \(B\).
Every cut is valid for the original feasible points in its node domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime preserves valid node lower bounds and cannot discard any feasible point solely through splitting or valid cutting.
review_flags: A source is needed for the precise split-cut regime and any convergence claim.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract branch-and-cut regime combining spatial subdivision with node-valid inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize an active list with the root domain and incumbent value \(U=+\infty\). For a selected node \(B\), solve \(R(B)\). If its lower bound is at least \(U\), discard \(B\). Otherwise, either add a node-valid inequality violated by the relaxation solution and resolve, or split \(B\) into covering children and construct their relaxations. Update \(U\) whenever a better feasible point is found. Terminate when the active list is empty or when \(U-\min_B\operatorname{lb}(R(B))\) satisfies the prescribed absolute or relative tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate valid cuts and covering spatial splits, pruning nodes by lower bounds until exhaustion or a certified optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Split-Cut Search Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The split-cut algorithm fits the leaf, but the precise lifecycle, pruning rule, and gap-termination regime require a supporting source.

children.title: Polynomial Spatial Global Search
children.top_down_role: Spatial search using polynomial reformulations and regional LP, conic, or semidefinite bounds.

children.title: Polynomial Reformulation Choices
children.top_down_role: Alternative polynomial representations affecting degree, sparsity, plus regional relaxation structure.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact and described by polynomial constraints.
Two lifted formulations project exactly onto the same original feasible set and preserve objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact reformulations have the same global optimum, but their finite regional relaxations may yield different lower bounds and computational costs.

notation.meaning: Projection from lifted to original variables.

review_flags: A source comparing spatial polynomial reformulations and their relaxation strength is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifting equivalence versus finite-relaxation strength in polynomial spatial search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) be lifted polynomial formulations satisfying \(\pi(F_1)=\pi(F_2)=K\), with lifted objectives equal to the original objective after projection. Then both exact formulations have the same global optimal value. If selected polynomial identities, auxiliary-variable equations, or integrality relations are relaxed to obtain \(R_1(B)\) and \(R_2(B)\) on a region \(B\), projection equivalence alone does not imply \(\inf R_1(B)=\inf R_2(B)\). Reformulation choice therefore determines relaxation dimension, separability, and regional bound strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent polynomial liftings preserve the exact optimum but can produce substantially different finite regional relaxations and computational burdens.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Reformulation Choices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits reformulation choices, but no source supports the relaxation-strength claims, and expressions such as inf R_i(B) require an explicitly defined relaxed objective problem rather than a bare relaxation object.

children.title: Regional LP Polynomial Bounds
children.top_down_role: Linear regional relaxations derived from polynomial structure over bounded domains.

assumptions_latex: \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\) with \(\ell_i<u_i\).
\(p\in\mathbb{R}[x]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any feasible \(\gamma\) satisfies \(\gamma\leq\min_{x\in B}p(x)\), so the optimal LP value is a certified regional lower bound.
review_flags: A source is needed for the selected box-generator LP certificate and degree-truncation convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Handelman-type LP positivity certificate on a bounded box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite index set \(I\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{2n}\). If coefficient matching verifies \[p(x)-\gamma=\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in I}c_{\alpha\beta}\prod_{i=1}^n(x_i-\ell_i)^{\alpha_i}(u_i-x_i)^{\beta_i},\qquad c_{\alpha\beta}\geq0,\] then every term on the right is nonnegative on \(B\). Maximizing \(\gamma\) subject to these coefficient equalities and nonnegativity constraints is a linear program. Increasing \(I\) enlarges the certificate cone but is not required for validity of any feasible bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative box-generator expansion of the shifted polynomial certifies a regional lower bound and can be found by linear programming.
knowledge_statements.title: Regional LP Polynomial Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind and finite Handelman-type box certificate are mathematically coherent, but the generator system and truncation convention have no citation.

children.title: Regional Conic Polynomial Bounds
children.top_down_role: Conic regional relaxations exploiting polynomial structure plus domain restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(K_B=\{x\in B:g_j(x)\geq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\).
All polynomials have degrees compatible with the selected truncated bases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible \(\gamma\) satisfies \(p(x)\geq\gamma\) on \(K_B\), and scaled-diagonal-dominance constraints permit conic optimization.
review_flags: A source is required for the SDSOS regional certificate, basis choice, and SOCP representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SDSOS-based second-order-cone certificate for a regional polynomial lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose coefficient matching establishes \[p(x)-\gamma=\sigma_0(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(x)g_j(x),\] where every \(\sigma_j\) has a Gram representation \(\sigma_j(x)=z_j(x)^{\mathsf T}Q_jz_j(x)\) with \(Q_j\) scaled diagonally dominant and positive semidefinite. Then every \(\sigma_j\) is nonnegative, so the identity certifies \(p(x)\geq\gamma\) for all \(x\in K_B\). With fixed monomial bases, maximizing \(\gamma\) under coefficient matching and scaled-diagonal-dominance constraints is representable as a second-order-cone program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SDSOS weighted constraint identity certifies a regional polynomial lower bound through a second-order-cone-representable Gram formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Regional Conic Polynomial Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SDSOS certificate and conic role fit the leaf, but the exact regional quadratic-module form, basis truncation, and SOCP representation require a source.

children.title: Regional Semidefinite Polynomial Bounds
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite regional relaxations used to strengthen polynomial lower bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(K_B=\{x\in B:g_j(x)\geq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\).
A finite relaxation order \(d\) fixes all multiplier degree limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any feasible \(\gamma\) is a certified lower bound on \(\min_{x\in K_B}p(x)\), and maximizing it is a semidefinite program.
review_flags: A source with the exact truncated quadratic-module regional formulation is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated SOS quadratic-module certificate on a spatial search region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At order \(d\), seek \(\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\) and sum-of-squares polynomials \(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_m\) satisfying \[p(x)-\gamma=\sigma_0(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(x)g_j(x),\qquad \deg(\sigma_jg_j)\leq2d.\] On \(K_B\), every term on the right is nonnegative, hence \(p(x)\geq\gamma\). Expressing each \(\sigma_j\) by a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix converts coefficient matching and maximization of \(\gamma\) into a semidefinite program. The certificate is valid at every feasible order, independently of hierarchy convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A truncated SOS identity with semialgebraic constraint multipliers gives an SDP-computable lower bound valid throughout the current region.
knowledge_statements.title: Regional Semidefinite Polynomial Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SOS certificate fits the semidefinite-bound leaf, but the cited support is absent and the displayed truncation must explicitly include the degree limit for sigma_0 as well as the weighted multipliers.

children.top_down_role: Implementation mechanisms affecting node throughput, numerical validity, and practical search robustness.
